name: Verbal Be-Passive
pattern: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + Head:VP[be + VP[past participle, complementᵢ externalized, optional internalized by-PP]]]

entry.name: Verbal Be-Passive
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + Head:VP[be + VP[past participle, complementᵢ externalized, optional internalized by-PP]]]

1.definition: Realigns the verb’s arguments so an internal complement of the active can appear as subject.
1.details: In my surfboard was stolen by Pat, the active object becomes subject, and a by-phrase realizes the participant that would be active subject. The short form usually leaves that participant unexpressed. The by-phrase can supply an experiencer when the active subject is an experiencer. The externalized complement can also come from a preposition, as in the paper was referred to. The participial VP may have complements and verbal modifications. This entry covers the auxiliary be construction.

examples.note: Long passive with the active subject expressed as the complement of by.

examples.form: [Her paper is referred to by everyone.]
examples.note: The active would express the paper as object of to.

relatedConstructions.notes: The be-passive is a voice construction available in headed clauses.
Both use a past participle, with different auxiliary selection and argument syntax.

grounds.note: Documents long and short passives and the complement correspondence.
Records auxiliary be followed by a past-participial form.

projection.target: A verbal be-passive lacks a complement present in the corresponding active VP. The missing complement can correspond to the passive subject, and a by-phrase can realize the active subject independently of its semantic role.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s active/passive comparisons include direct objects, indirect objects, prepositional objects and non-agent subjects. CASA records the auxiliary and participle pairing.

curious.title: Putting the receiver first
curious.summary: In a passive sentence, the object of the matching active sentence becomes the subject, and the active sentence's subject can come later after by or be left out.
curious.body:
In My surfboard was stolen by Pat, the surfboard comes first, though it's what Pat stole. The person who acted appears after by. In My surfboard was stolen, the doer is simply left out.

The first thing can come from other places too. In Her paper is referred to by everyone, the paper is what everyone refers to, and the active version has it after the word to. This dictionary covers the passives made with the helper verb be, followed by a word like stolen.

examples.text: [Her paper is referred to by everyone.]

curious.try: Take an active sentence like Pat stole my surfboard and turn it around. What happens to Pat?

teacher.summary: Explains the be-passive as a way of realigning a verb's arguments so an active complement becomes the subject.
teacher.explain: In the verbal be-passive, an internal complement of the active verb appears as the subject, and the participial VP lacks that complement. A by-phrase can realize the participant that would be the active subject, and the short passive usually leaves that participant unexpressed. The externalized complement can be a direct object, an indirect object, or the object of a preposition, as in the paper was referred to. The by-phrase can supply an experiencer when the active subject is an experiencer. The participial VP may have complements and verbal modifications. Only the construction with auxiliary be is covered here.
teacher.terms: Long passive has a by-phrase, and short passive has none. Such clauses are sometimes said to be in the passive voice; this dictionary calls the version with be the verbal be-passive.

examples.text: [Her paper is referred to by everyone.]

contrasts.text: My surfboard was stolen by Pat.
contrasts.note: Long passive; the active subject is the complement of by.

watch_for: A learner might think the by-phrase is required, when a short passive can leave that participant out.
A learner might expect only a direct object to become the subject, when a prepositional object can too (Her paper is referred to).
teacher.activity: Students turn active sentences into long passives and then short passives. They say which participant becomes the subject and where the original subject went.

child.hook: In "My surfboard was stolen", who is missing from the sentence?
child.explain: You can start a sentence with the thing something happened to. My surfboard was stolen by Pat. If we don't need to say who did it, we can leave out by Pat.
child.play: Make up a sentence like Pat stole my surfboard. Turn it around so the thing comes first. Then try it without the doer.
